compensation.sign_on_bonus_clawback: Full repayment if employment ends for any reason within 24 months, due within 30 days of termination (Section 3.4).
compensation.lab_fee_deduction: Lab fees, implant/specialty supply costs, refunds, and chargebacks are deducted from collections before the 30% split (Section 3.3).

restrictive_covenants.non_compete_scope: Practicing dentistry within 15 miles of ANY employer or affiliate office where the provider worked even once — not just the home office (Section 7.1).
restrictive_covenants.liquidated_damages: $100,000 liquidated damages for breach, plus injunctive relief (Section 7.3).

term_and_termination.for_cause_provisions: For-cause triggers include failure to meet unspecified production standards and conduct 'in Employer's sole judgment' detrimental to reputation (Section 6.2) — broad and subjective.

benefits.tail_coverage_paid_by: Provider, at provider's sole expense, on termination for any reason (Section 5).
benefits.health_insurance: Eligible for group health plan per plan terms.
benefits.retirement: Eligible for 401(k) per plan terms; no match specified.
benefits.ce_allowance: $500 per year; no paid CE days specified.

extraction.patient_records_ownership: All patient records, charts, and goodwill belong solely to the employer (Section 8).
other_notable_clauses: Employer may reassign the provider to other locations it 'reasonably designates' (Section 1).
Clinical judgment clause is qualified by required compliance with employer treatment-planning protocols (Section 9).

summary: This is a two-year associate dentist offer from BrightSmile Dental Partners, a DSO in Frisco, Texas. Pay is a $650 daily guarantee for only the first 90 days, after which you are paid 30% of net collections — meaning 30% of what the office actually collects for your work, after lab fees and supply costs are subtracted. It includes a $15,000 signing bonus with a two-year full-repayment clawback, a 24-month/15-mile non-compete measured from every office you ever work at, and claims-made malpractice insurance where you pay for tail coverage yourself when you leave.
strengths: The 30% rate itself is within the normal range for DSO associate agreements.
A daily guarantee during ramp-up is standard and $650/day is a reasonable floor while it lasts.
The $15,000 signing bonus is a real benefit if you stay the full two years.
Health insurance and 401(k) eligibility are included.

red_flags.title: Pay is based on collections, with deductions taken before your split
red_flags.explanation: You are paid on what the office collects, not what you produce. If the office bills $30,000 for your work but only collects $24,000 — and then subtracts lab fees and implant supplies — your 30% applies to the smaller number. You bear the risk of the office's billing and collections performance, and lab-heavy procedures (crowns, implants) can pay you dramatically less than expected.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for the office's historical collection rate in writing, and ask whether the split can be based on production (or collections before lab-fee deductions). Attorneys commonly negotiate lab fees to be deducted after the split or shared.

red_flags.title: You pay your own malpractice tail coverage
red_flags.explanation: The employer provides claims-made insurance, which only covers claims filed while the policy is active. When you leave — even if they fire you — you must buy 'tail' coverage covering later-filed claims, at your own expense. Tail policies commonly cost one to two times the annual premium, which can be thousands of dollars due right when you're changing jobs.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask the employer to pay the tail (or split it, or cover it if they terminate you without cause). This is one of the most commonly negotiated clauses in healthcare contracts.

red_flags.title: Non-compete measured from every office you ever touch
red_flags.explanation: The 15-mile, 24-month restriction applies around any employer or affiliate office where you provided services 'on one or more occasions.' If they float you to several offices, the restricted zones stack and can blanket an entire metro area, severely limiting where you can work next.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask to limit the non-compete to your primary office only, and to have it waived if the employer terminates you without cause. An attorney can also assess enforceability under Texas law.

red_flags.title: $100,000 liquidated damages for covenant breach
red_flags.explanation: Beyond the non-compete itself, breaching it triggers an automatic $100,000 payment plus court orders. This is a large, fixed penalty that applies regardless of how much harm (if any) the employer actually suffered.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for this clause to be removed or substantially reduced — this is squarely a question for your attorney before signing.

red_flags.title: Sign-on bonus is fully repayable for two years, even if they fire you
red_flags.explanation: The $15,000 must be repaid in full if employment ends 'for any reason' within 24 months — including the employer terminating you without cause on 30 days' notice. There is also no pro-rating: leaving in month 23 costs the same as leaving in month 2.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for the clawback to pro-rate monthly and to be waived if the employer terminates without cause.

red_flags.title: Vague for-cause termination triggers
red_flags.explanation: The employer can fire you immediately for failing 'production standards' that aren't defined anywhere, or for conduct they alone judge harmful to their reputation. Vague triggers like these can convert a without-cause firing (with notice) into a for-cause one (immediate, and reputationally worse).
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for production standards to be defined in writing and for a cure period — written notice and 15-30 days to fix the issue — before for-cause termination.

red_flags.title: Notice periods are lopsided: they give 30 days, you give 90
red_flags.explanation: The employer can end the agreement on 30 days' notice while you must give 90. Combined with the 90-day non-renewal window and auto-renewal, leaving cleanly requires careful calendar math.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask to make notice periods mutual — 60/60 or 90/90.

red_flags.title: Thin PTO and CE support
red_flags.explanation: Five PTO days and $500 of CE per year are on the low end for associate positions; many offers include 10+ days and $1,500-3,000 in CE with dedicated CE days.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for additional PTO and a larger CE allowance — these are low-cost items employers often concede.

red_flags.title: Employer owns all patient records and goodwill
red_flags.explanation: Standard for DSO agreements, but combined with the patient non-solicit it means the patients you build relationships with cannot follow you when you leave.
red_flags.what_to_do: Understand this going in; ask whether departing providers may notify patients of their departure, which some states require regardless of contract.

negotiation_points.rationale: Collections-based pay with pre-split lab-fee deductions is the single biggest driver of lower-than-expected take-home for new associates.
negotiation_points.suggested_ask: Would you be open to basing my percentage on adjusted production, or alternatively deducting lab fees after the split? I'd also appreciate the office's collection-rate history for the past year.

negotiation_points.rationale: Provider-paid tail is a multi-thousand-dollar exit cost and is very commonly shifted to the employer in negotiation.
negotiation_points.suggested_ask: I'd like the agreement to provide employer-paid tail coverage, or at minimum employer-paid tail if my employment is terminated without cause.

negotiation_points.rationale: Ninety days is a short ramp for a new practice; new patient flow and credentialing often take longer, and a longer floor protects you while your schedule fills.
negotiation_points.suggested_ask: Given typical ramp-up time, would you extend the $650 daily guarantee to the first 6 months?

negotiation_points.rationale: As written, the restriction stacks around every office you ever cover, which can lock you out of the whole metro.
negotiation_points.suggested_ask: Can we limit the non-compete to my primary practice location, and waive it entirely if I'm terminated without cause?

negotiation_points.rationale: A pro-rated, no-fault-protected clawback is the market norm; full repayment after 23 months, or after being fired, is not.
negotiation_points.suggested_ask: Could the signing-bonus repayment pro-rate monthly over the 24 months, and be waived if the company terminates me without cause?

questions_for_attorney: Is the stacked non-compete in Section 7.1 (15 miles from every office I ever work at, for 24 months) likely enforceable under Texas law, and can it be narrowed?
Is the $100,000 liquidated-damages clause in Section 7.3 enforceable, and what is my realistic exposure?
Does Section 6.2's 'sole judgment' for-cause language give the employer effectively unlimited termination discretion, and can we add defined standards and a cure period?
How should the tail-coverage obligation in Section 5 be quantified before I sign — what would tail actually cost for this policy?
Does the 'Net Collections' definition in Section 3.3 allow any other deductions beyond lab fees and supplies that I should cap in writing?
Are there Texas-specific rules on patient notification or record access that override Section 8 when a dentist departs?
overall_read: This offer has a market-typical headline (30% with a $650/day floor and a $15,000 bonus) attached to below-market fine print: collections-based pay with pre-split lab deductions, provider-paid tail, a stacking metro-wide non-compete with a $100,000 penalty, and a two-year full clawback. Offers like this are frequently improved substantially in negotiation — the biggest items to resolve before signing are the compensation basis, the tail coverage, and the non-compete scope, all of which are standard asks an attorney can help you frame.
